prose.hook: Malaysia is split across two landmasses: a peninsula bordering Thailand and the northern third of the island of Borneo, separated by the South China Sea. That geography puts it astride the Strait of Malacca, one of the world's busiest shipping corridors, and underpins an economy built on integrated circuits, petroleum, natural gas, and palm oil.
prose.physicalGeography: The country's territory consists of coastal plains rising to hills and mountains, split between Peninsular Malaysia and the northern third of Borneo. Both parts border Indonesia and Brunei, with the South China Sea separating the peninsula from the Borneo territories.
prose.climate: Malaysia's tropical climate is shaped by two annual monsoons: a southwest monsoon from April to October and a northeast monsoon from October to February. These seasonal shifts bring recurring flooding and landslides, and forest fires are also a hazard.
prose.economy: Malaysia is an upper middle-income Southeast Asian economy with high labor productivity, and its trade sector employs over 40% of jobs. It is a major exporter of electronics, oil, and chemicals, with integrated circuits, refined and crude petroleum, natural gas, and palm oil among its top exports. Industry varies by region: Peninsular Malaysia focuses on rubber and oil palm processing, petroleum and gas, electronics and semiconductors, and pharmaceuticals, while Sabah and Sarawak rely more on logging, agriculture processing, and petroleum and natural gas production.
prose.peopleAndCulture: Malaysia's population is majority Muslim (63.5%), with significant Buddhist (18.7%), Christian (9.1%), and Hindu (6.1%) minorities, alongside smaller communities practicing Confucianism, Taoism, and other traditional Chinese religions. Ethnically, Bumiputera make up 63.8% of the population, including Malays and indigenous peoples such as the Orang Asli, Dayak, and Anak Negeri, with Chinese (20.6%) and Indian (6%) communities forming substantial minorities alongside a non-citizen population of 9%.
